newsitem.title: FRANCE: French guide restores top rating to two kitchens.
newsitem.headline: French guide restores top rating to two kitchens.

text.p: The Gault-Millau restaurant guide to France has restored its highest rating to two restaurants which fell out of favour in last year's edition, Gault-Millau said on Tuesday.

The 1997 guide restored its coveted rating of four "toques" -- the traditional towering white chef's cap -- to Marc Meneau's L'Esperance in Saint-Pere-sous-Vezelay in central France and Alain Passard's L'Arpege in Paris.

Two other super-chefs -- Joel Robuchon in Paris and Pierre Gagnaire in Saint-Etienne, central France -- were dropped from the top category because they had closed their doors, leaving a dozen restaurants in the highest category for a second year.
The guide singled out for special honour Jacques Chibois, chef and owner of La Bastide Saint Antoine in the southern French resort town of Grasse, naming him its chef of the year.
The restaurant, which opened its doors just seven months ago, specialises in the cuisine of Provence and offers dinner without wine at about 380 to 600 francs ($75 to $120).
Chibois, who is 43, was previously chef at the Grey d'Albion luxury hotel in the Riviera city Cannes.
The guide said it gave special emphasis this year to moderately priced restaurants offering diners good value for their money.

The French restaurant industry's enduring financial crisis "has brought to the fore a new generation of chefs who know how to provide creative cooking at good value," Gault-Millau said in a statement.
"Today, young chefs born out of the crisis know that a bill of 150 to 200 francs ($30 to $40) does not prevent them from using their imagination," the guide's authors said.

The most exclusive French restaurants have been badly shaken by tough financial times in recent years, forcing them to cut back on costs, sell processed foods and kitchenware on the side or open cheaper bistros next door in order to remain afloat.
Gagnaire in January became the first top-rated chef in France to be forced into bankruptcy. He has since announced plans to open a more modest restaurant in Paris.
Robuchon retired at age 51, turning over his Paris restaurant to chef Alain Ducasse, who also runs the kitchen at the Louis XV in Monaco.

The latest Gault-Millau guide for France steered clear of the controversy triggered by last year's edition, which slashed the number of restaurants given its highest rating to a dozen from 30 after concluding that most were overrated.
The rival Michelin guide, France's most prestigious restaurant guide, bestowed its highest award of three stars to 19 restaurants last year, down from 20 in 1995.
Both L'Esperance and L'Arpege had three-star ratings in the Michelin 1996 guide. The 1997 edition is due out early next year.
